title: Probability & Statistics
blurb: Unit-by-unit practice for the Probability & Statistics course — counting to inference, every unit with its own exercise set.

units.title: Counting Principles
units.blurb: The multiplication and addition principles, complementary counting, and organized lists — how to count without counting.

units.title: Permutations & Arrangements
units.blurb: Factorials, arrangements of all or some objects, repeated letters, and seating with restrictions.

units.title: Combinations
units.blurb: Choosing without order: nCr, committees, at-least and at-most counts, and when order matters vs when it doesn't.

units.title: Pascal's Triangle & the Binomial Theorem
units.blurb: The triangle that counts everything: binomial coefficients, expanding powers, and finding specific terms.

units.title: Probability Models
units.blurb: Sample spaces, events, equally-likely outcomes, complements, and the addition rule with Venn diagrams.

units.title: Conditional Probability & Independence
units.blurb: How information changes chance: P(A|B), the multiplication rule, independence, weighted trees, and Bayes by table.

units.title: Random Variables & Expected Value
units.blurb: Turning outcomes into numbers: probability distributions, expected value, variance, and what makes a game fair.

units.title: The Binomial Distribution
units.blurb: Repeated independent trials: binomial probabilities, expected count np, shape, and simulation.

units.title: Describing Data
units.blurb: Center and spread done right: mean, median, IQR, standard deviation, boxplots, and the 1.5×IQR outlier fence.

units.title: Distribution Shape & Position
units.blurb: Histograms and shape, percentiles, z-scores, and the normal curve with the 68–95–99.7 rule.

units.title: Two-Variable Data
units.blurb: Scatterplots, the correlation coefficient, the least-squares line, and why correlation is not causation.

units.title: Sampling, Studies & Inference
units.blurb: Random sampling, bias, experiments vs observation, simulation-based inference, and margin of error — the capstone.

forms.title: Multi-stage journeys
forms.skill: Each leg multiplies; adding counts single roads.

variants.statement: A journey has $2$ routes to town A, $3$ on to town B, and $4$ on to town C. How many complete journeys are there?
variants.explanation: Each leg multiplies: $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$. Stopping at $6$ counts journeys only as far as B, and adding the legs counts single roads rather than whole journeys.

forms.title: The multiplication principle
forms.skill: Independent choices multiply: each option pairs with every other.

variants.statement: From $4$ different letters, how many strings of length $3$ can be made if letters MAY repeat?
variants.explanation: Every one of the $3$ positions has all $4$ letters available, so the count is $4^{3} = 64$. Forbidding repeats would shrink the pool at each step and give $24$ instead.

forms.title: Add or multiply?
forms.skill: OR means add the counts; AND (one of each) means multiply.

variants.statement: A locker code consists of one letter chosen from $4$ letters followed by one digit chosen from $10$ digits. How many different codes are possible?
variants.explanation: The code needs a letter AND a digit, so the choices multiply: $4 \cdot 10 = 40$. Adding $4 + 10 = 14$ is the classic slip — that counts picking just one symbol.

forms.title: Complementary counting
forms.skill: Count the opposite and subtract — it beats counting overlaps.

variants.statement: A code has $2$ characters, each chosen from $5$ symbols. How many codes use the first symbol AT LEAST once?
variants.explanation: Count the opposite and subtract. Codes AVOIDING that symbol use the other $4$ everywhere: $4^{2} = 16$. So the ones that use it are $25 - 16 = 9$. Counting directly means counting overlaps twice.

forms.title: Arrangements with a fixed block
forms.skill: Only the unfixed people can be rearranged.

variants.statement: In how many orders can $5$ people line up if $2$ named people must take the first $2$ places in a fixed order?
variants.explanation: The first $2$ places are decided, so only the remaining $3$ people can be rearranged: $3! = 6$. The unrestricted count would be $5! = 120$.

variants.statement: In how many orders can $6$ people line up if $2$ named people must take the first $2$ places in a fixed order?

forms.title: Permutations nPr
forms.skill: Order matters: n!/(n−r)! counts arrangements.

variants.statement: Compute $P(5, 2)$ — the number of ways to arrange $2$ of $5$ distinct objects in a row.
variants.explanation: $P(5, 2) = \frac{5!}{(5 - 2)!} = 20$. Dividing by $2!$ as well gives $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ — that counts unordered choices, not arrangements.

variants.statement: A class has $5$ boys and $6$ girls. In how many ways can a committee of exactly $2$ boys and $3$ girls be chosen?

variants.statement: The probability that it rains tomorrow is $\frac{2}{5}$. What is the probability that it does not rain?

forms.title: Two draws without replacement

variants.statement: A bag holds $10$ balls of which $4$ are red. Two are drawn WITHOUT replacement. What is the probability both are red?
variants.explanation: The first draw is $\frac{4}{10}$; the second is out of a smaller bag with one red gone: $\frac{3}{9}$. Multiplying gives $\frac{2}{15}$. Using $\frac{4}{10}$ twice would assume the ball was replaced.

forms.title: Independent AND

variants.statement: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $P(B) = \frac{2}{3}$. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
variants.explanation: Independent events multiply: $P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$. The formula $P(A) + P(B) - P(A)P(B) = \frac{5}{6}$ computes $P(A \cup B)$ — the OR, not the AND.

variants.statement: A school has $40$ students; $16$ of them play chess, and $6$ of the chess players are girls. One chess player is chosen at random. What is the probability that a girl is chosen?

forms.title: Testing independence
forms.skill: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B), or they are dependent.

variants.statement: $P(A) = \frac{1}{2}$, $P(B) = \frac{1}{3}$ and $P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{6}$. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?
options: yes — because both probabilities are less than $1$
variants.explanation: Independence is exactly the test $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$. Here $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6}$, and the given intersection is $\frac{1}{6}$ — so they are independent. Overlapping is not the same as being dependent.

forms.title: Conditioning the other way
forms.skill: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are different numbers.

variants.statement: In a survey, $20$ people both cycle and commute, $5$ cycle but do not commute, $10$ commute without cycling and $65$ do neither. Given someone COMMUTES, what is the probability they cycle?
variants.explanation: The condition is COMMUTES, so the population shrinks to the $20 + 10 = 30$ commuters, of whom $20$ cycle: $\frac{2}{3}$. Conditioning the other way round — on cycling — gives $\frac{20}{25}$, a genuinely different number.

forms.title: Expected gain per play

variants.statement: A game costs $1$ togrog to play. You win $5$ togrog if a fair $6$-sided die shows its highest face, and nothing otherwise. What is the expected gain per play?
variants.explanation: The expected WINNINGS are $\frac{5}{6}$, and the cost is paid every time, so the expected gain is $\frac{5}{6} - 1 = -\frac{1}{6}$. Forgetting to subtract the cost is what makes a losing game look profitable.

forms.title: Exactly k successes
forms.skill: P = C(n,k) p^k (1−p)^(n−k) — the C(n,k) counts the orders.

variants.statement: A fair coin is flipped $3$ times. What is the probability of getting exactly $1$ heads?
variants.explanation: There are $\binom{3}{1} = 3$ orders for the heads among $2^{3} = 8$ equally likely outcomes, so $P = \frac{3}{8}$. Answering $\frac{1}{8}$ forgets the $\binom{3}{1}$ orderings.

variants.statement: A fair die is rolled $3$ times. What is the probability that it shows a five or a six on exactly $1$ of the rolls?
variants.explanation: Each roll succeeds with $p = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$, so $P = \binom{3}{1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2} = \frac{4}{9}$. Swapping the exponents gives $\frac{2}{9}$ — success and failure traded places.

forms.title: Mean and median
forms.skill: Mean: sum ÷ count. Median: middle of the SORTED list.

variants.statement: Find the mean of the data set: $7$, $2$, $9$, $4$, $3$.
variants.explanation: Add and divide by the count: $\frac{7 + 2 + 9 + 4 + 3}{5} = 5$. The middle value of the sorted list, $4$, is the median — a different statistic.

variants.statement: Find the mean of the data set: $12$, $3$, $9$, $5$, $1$.
variants.explanation: Add and divide by the count: $\frac{12 + 3 + 9 + 5 + 1}{5} = 6$. The middle value of the sorted list, $5$, is the median — a different statistic.

forms.title: Median of an even count

variants.statement: What is the median of $2,\ 5,\ 8,\ 15$?
variants.explanation: With an EVEN count there is no single middle value, so average the two in the middle: $\frac{5 + 8}{2} = \frac{13}{2}$. Picking just one of them is the usual slip, and the mean $\frac{15}{2}$ is a different measure again.

variants.statement: For the data $5,\ 7,\ 7,\ 14,\ 22$, what is the range?
variants.explanation: The range is the largest minus the smallest: $22 - 5 = 17$. The mode — the most frequent value — is $7$, which measures something quite different.

forms.title: How a new value moves the mean

variants.statement: The mean of $4$ numbers is $10$. After one more number, $20$, is added to the list, what is the new mean?
variants.explanation: The old numbers total $4 \cdot 10 = 40$, so the new mean is $\frac{40 + 20}{5} = 12$. Averaging just $10$ and $20$ pretends the list held a single number.

forms.title: Weighted means
forms.skill: Divide by the total weight, not by the count.

variants.statement: A course scores $80$ on a paper worth $3$ credits and $60$ on a paper worth $2$ credits. What is the weighted mean?
variants.explanation: Weight each score by its credits, then divide by the TOTAL credits: $\frac{80 \cdot 3 + 60 \cdot 2}{5} = 72$. The plain average $70$ ignores that the papers count for different amounts.

variants.statement: A set of $4$ values all equal $20$. A new value of $100$ is added. By how much does the MEAN rise?
variants.explanation: The mean was $20$ and becomes $\frac{80 + 100}{5} = 36$, a rise of $16$. Note the new value sits $80$ above the old mean but moves it far less, because it is shared across $5$ values.

forms.title: Reading skew

variants.statement: A distribution has mean $70$ and median $62$. Which way is it skewed?
options: not at all — it is symmetric

variants.explanation: The mean is dragged toward the long tail while the median stays put, so mean above median means the tail lies to the right. Here $70$ > $62$.

forms.title: Shifting every value

variants.statement: Every value in a data set with mean $12$ and standard deviation $5$ has $10$ ADDED to it. What is the new standard deviation?
variants.explanation: Adding a constant slides every value the same distance, so the SPREAD is untouched: the standard deviation stays $5$. The MEAN does move, from $12$ to $22$ — which is the number most people adjust by mistake.

variants.statement: What correlation would you expect between hours revised and exam mark?
variants.explanation: As hours revised rises, exam mark tends to rise too, which is positive correlation. Note that no real data set reaches exactly $1$ — that would mean the points sit on a perfect straight line.

variants.statement: What correlation would you expect between hours of television and exam mark?
variants.explanation: As hours of television rises, exam mark tends to fall, which is negative correlation. Note that no real data set reaches exactly $1$ — that would mean the points sit on a perfect straight line.

variants.statement: What correlation would you expect between shoe size and exam mark?

forms.title: Reading a scatterplot's trend

variants.statement: A scatterplot compares hours a student studies ($x$) with the score they earn on the exam ($y$). As $x$ increases, $y$ tends to INCREASE. Which best describes the association?
variants.explanation: Here both variables rise together, so the cloud of points slopes upward. A real scatterplot is rarely a PERFECT line — association describes the overall trend, not an exact fit.

variants.statement: A scatterplot compares a car's age in years ($x$) with its resale value ($y$). As $x$ increases, $y$ tends to DECREASE. Which best describes the association?

forms.title: Correlation against cause
forms.skill: A lurking variable or a reversed arrow explains most links.

variants.statement: Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer. What is the safest conclusion?
options: correlation is not proof of cause here — a lurking variable — hot weather — drives both
the first definitely causes the second
the second definitely causes the first
variants.explanation: An observed association can arise from a lurking variable, from the causal arrow pointing the other way, or from chance. Here, a lurking variable — hot weather — drives both — so a causal claim is not safe on this evidence alone.

correlation is not proof of cause here — both simply track how big the town is
the second definitely causes the first

forms.title: What the slope means
forms.skill: The slope is a rate of change; the intercept is the starting value.

variants.statement: A fitted line is $y = 7x + 3$, where $x$ is kilometres driven and $y$ is litres of fuel used. What does the $7$ tell you?
options: each extra unit of kilometres driven adds about $7$ to litres of fuel used
the value of litres of fuel used when kilometres driven is zero
the total litres of fuel used across the whole data set
how well the line fits the points
variants.explanation: The slope is a RATE OF CHANGE: one more unit of kilometres driven is associated with about $7$ more of litres of fuel used. The intercept $3$ is the value when kilometres driven is zero, and the fit is measured separately.

forms.title: Naming a sampling method
forms.skill: Stratified samples within groups; cluster takes whole groups.

variants.statement: Which sampling method is this? Numbering everyone and picking with a random number table.
variants.explanation: Simple random sampling. Stratified sampling splits into groups and samples WITHIN each; cluster sampling picks whole groups and takes everyone in them — that is the pair most often confused.

variants.statement: Which sampling method is this? Taking every $10$th name on an alphabetical list.
variants.explanation: Systematic sampling. Stratified sampling splits into groups and samples WITHIN each; cluster sampling picks whole groups and takes everyone in them — that is the pair most often confused.

variants.statement: Which sampling method is this? Splitting by year group and sampling randomly within each.
variants.explanation: Stratified sampling. Stratified sampling splits into groups and samples WITHIN each; cluster sampling picks whole groups and takes everyone in them — that is the pair most often confused.

variants.statement: Which sampling method is this? Picking a few whole classes at random and surveying everyone in them.
variants.explanation: Cluster sampling. Stratified sampling splits into groups and samples WITHIN each; cluster sampling picks whole groups and takes everyone in them — that is the pair most often confused.

variants.explanation: Convenience sampling. Stratified sampling splits into groups and samples WITHIN each; cluster sampling picks whole groups and takes everyone in them — that is the pair most often confused.

forms.title: What kind of study is this?
forms.skill: Assigning → experiment; watching → observational; everyone → census; a subset → sample survey.

variants.statement: A researcher randomly ASSIGNS half of 60 plants to a new fertilizer and half to none, then compares growth. This is best described as…
variants.explanation: Here the researcher ASSIGNS the treatment — that active assignment is exactly what makes it an experiment. Assignment → experiment; watching → observational; everyone → census; a chosen subset → sample survey.

variants.statement: A doctor reviews EXISTING hospital records to compare recovery times of two treatments patients already chose. This is best described as…
variants.explanation: Here no treatment is assigned; existing behavior is only watched or looked up. Assignment → experiment; watching → observational; everyone → census; a chosen subset → sample survey.

variants.statement: The school asks EVERY SINGLE student in the building which lunch option they prefer. This is best described as…
variants.explanation: Here EVERY member of the group is measured, not a subset. Assignment → experiment; watching → observational; everyone → census; a chosen subset → sample survey.

variants.statement: A pollster RANDOMLY SELECTS 400 of a city's voters and asks whom they support. This is best described as…
variants.explanation: Here a random SUBSET of the population answers — a sample standing in for the whole. Assignment → experiment; watching → observational; everyone → census; a chosen subset → sample survey.

variants.statement: A lab randomly ASSIGNS volunteers to sleep 6 or 8 hours, then measures reaction time. This is best described as…
variants.explanation: Here the researcher ASSIGNS the treatment — that active assignment is exactly what makes it an experiment. Assignment → experiment; watching → observational; everyone → census; a chosen subset → sample survey.

forms.title: From sample to population
forms.skill: Scale the sample proportion up to the population size.

variants.statement: A city has $12000$ residents. In a random sample of $200$ residents, $45$ approve of a new park. What is the best estimate of the TOTAL number of residents who approve?
variants.explanation: Scale the sample rate up to the population: $\frac{45}{200} \cdot 12000 = 2700$. The raw count $45$ describes only the sample, not the whole city.

forms.title: Spotting bias
forms.skill: A structural flaw does not shrink with a bigger sample.

variants.statement: What is the main problem with this study? A survey on library use is conducted inside the library.
options: the sample over-represents people who already use libraries
the sample is too small to say anything
the results should be reported as percentages
variants.explanation: The flaw is structural rather than a matter of size: the sample over-represents people who already use libraries. Adding more people would not fix it, because every extra person is drawn from the same skewed pool.

variants.statement: What is the main problem with this study? A poll about phone habits is run by text message.
options: the sample is too small to say anything

the results should be reported as percentages
variants.explanation: The flaw is structural rather than a matter of size: people without phones cannot answer at all. Adding more people would not fix it, because every extra person is drawn from the same skewed pool.

forms.title: Population, sample, parameter, statistic

variants.statement: In a study, what is all $40\,000$ voters in a district?

forms.title: Permutations against combinations

variants.statement: From $5$ distinct items, how many ORDERED arrangements of $3$ are there?
variants.explanation: Order matters, so this is a permutation: $P(5,3) = \frac{5!}{(5-3)!} = 60$. The combination $C(5,3) = 10$ counts the same selections while IGNORING order, which is why it is $3!$ times smaller.

variants.statement: From $5$ distinct items, how many UNORDERED selections of $3$ are there?

forms.title: The binomial distribution
forms.skill: Choose WHICH trials succeed, then weight successes and failures.

variants.statement: A trial succeeds with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. In $3$ independent trials, find $P(\text{exactly } 1 \text{ successes})$.
variants.explanation: The binomial formula is $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$: $\binom{3}{1} = 3$ ways to choose WHICH trials succeed, times $\frac{1}{2}^{1}$ for those successes, times $\frac{1}{2}^{2}$ for the failures, giving $\frac{3}{8}$. Dropping the coefficient counts only one specific ordering.

variants.statement: A trial succeeds with probability $\frac{1}{3}$. In $3$ independent trials, find $P(\text{exactly } 1 \text{ successes})$.
variants.explanation: The binomial formula is $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$: $\binom{3}{1} = 3$ ways to choose WHICH trials succeed, times $\frac{1}{3}^{1}$ for those successes, times $\frac{2}{3}^{2}$ for the failures, giving $\frac{4}{9}$. Dropping the coefficient counts only one specific ordering.

variants.statement: A random variable takes the value $10$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ and $20$ with probability $\frac{3}{4}$. Find its expected value.
variants.explanation: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability: $\frac{1}{4}(10) + \frac{3}{4}(20) = \frac{35}{2}$. The plain average $15$ would be right only if the two outcomes were equally likely.

forms.title: z-scores
forms.skill: How many standard deviations from the mean, with the sign kept.

variants.statement: A distribution has mean $100$ and standard deviation $15$. Find the $z$-score of the value $70$.
variants.explanation: A $z$-score counts standard deviations from the mean: $z = \frac{70 - 100}{15} = \frac{-30}{15} = -2$. The sign says which side of the mean the value sits on, so reversing the subtraction reverses the meaning.
